The problem PRIME was built for did not go away. **What happened instead is stranger and is the organising fact of this survey. The capability was demonstrated, it was adopted, it was then given up by the very class of vehicle it had been built for, and it was adopted again by a different class of vehicle for the opposite reason.**

The field as it currently stands is large, since 2,237 of the survey's research records were published in 2010 or later, and the clusters below divide it by subject.

### The Vehicles It Was Built For Gave the Capability Up

**Every crewed spacecraft flying to orbit today comes home as a blunt capsule, as Mercury did.** The Space Shuttle is the only crewed spaceplane to have flown in orbit, and Orion, Dragon, Soyuz and Shenzhou are the current capsules, in the [encyclopaedia entry on space capsules][ref_space_capsule], and the literature of that choice is gathered below under capsules and ballistic entry.

The relation derived here is still the quickest way to see what that costs. A blunt capsule trims at a lift-to-drag ratio near 0.3, a nominal value assumed here, and the crossrange it yields is

$$
y = \pi^2/48 \times 0.3^2 \times 6.371\times 10^6 = 118\ \text{km}
\tag{85}
$$

or 117 kilometres by the exact integration, the two being close here because at so small a lift-to-drag ratio the heading barely turns and the small-angle step costs almost nothing. Set against the once-per-orbit requirement of 1,254 kilometres derived earlier, that is

$$
\frac{117}{1{,}254} = 0.09
\tag{86}
$$

**Nine percent.** A modern crewed spacecraft has, by deliberate choice, about one eleventh of the crossrange that would let it come home when it wants to.

The ratios in the table are nominal values assumed for illustration. The lifting-body rows sit within the 1.0 to 1.4 that [Reed][research_r_dale_reed_1997] gives for the piloted lifting bodies.

| Vehicle | Lift-to-drag ratio | Crossrange, exact |
|---|---|---|
| A ballistic capsule with no lift | 0 | 0 km |
| Mercury and Vostok | 0.05 | 3 km |
| Apollo, Orion and Soyuz | 0.30 | 117 km |
| PRIME, at the lower disputed figure | 1.00 | 1,214 km |
| The Space Shuttle orbiter | 1.10 | 1,447 km |
| The X-24A | 1.40 | 2,233 km |

**The regression came from the requirement disappearing, and engineering did not fail.** The once-around polar mission that generated the Shuttle's 1,100 nautical miles was an Air Force requirement, in [Heppenheimer][ref_heppenheimer_1999], and when Shuttle operations from Vandenberg were cancelled before they began, in the [history of Space Launch Complex 6][ref_vandenberg_slc6], nothing else needed that number. An ocean landing needs no runway, a parachute weighs less than a wing, and a capsule's heat shield is a simpler object than an orbiter's. **The Shuttle's wing was the last time crossrange drove a crewed vehicle's shape**, and PRIME is part of the reason that wing could be drawn with confidence.

### Crossrange Became a Weapon's Virtue

The capability did not disappear. It moved to weapons, whose literature appears below under hypersonic glide vehicles, their tracking and their interception.

**A hypersonic glide vehicle wants lateral range for exactly the reason a spacecraft did not.** A returning spacecraft wanted to reach a chosen site. A glide vehicle wants a trajectory that cannot be extrapolated, because an interceptor must be committed early and a manoeuvring target invalidates the prediction it was committed against. The literature reflects that inversion, being largely about estimating and tracking a manoeuvring entry body, where the period literature was about designing one.

**The relation is the same and the motive is not, and the equation cannot tell the difference.** The derivation above contains nothing that distinguishes a landing site from an evasive manoeuvre.

One limit constrains the treatment given here, though not the literature. A slender glide vehicle may reach a lift-to-drag ratio of 2.5, which [Reed][research_r_dale_reed_1997] reports for the slender lifting bodies, and the closed form would offer 8,187 kilometres for it. **That number should not be believed.** At such a ratio the closed form over-predicts by 41 percent, the accumulated heading change passes 400 degrees, and even the exact constant-bank integration is describing a trajectory no vehicle would fly. **The relation that describes PRIME does not describe its successors**, and saying so is more useful than extrapolating it past its assumptions.

### The Computation Became Free

**What changed most is not the physics but the cost of solving it**, as the cluster below on entry guidance, trajectory optimisation and hypersonic flight control shows.

The crossrange relation derived above is a closed form obtained by forcing the trajectory to be an equilibrium glide at constant bank. That was necessary in 1964 because the alternative was unaffordable. The modern equivalent solves the trajectory numerically, onboard, in real time, and increasingly by convex optimisation whose convergence can be guaranteed rather than hoped for. **It arrives at very nearly the same answer, because the physics did not move.**

**The closed form's role has changed rather than ended.** It is no longer how a vehicle is sized. It is now how an optimiser's answer is checked, the same use made of it above.

### The Ablator Is Computed Rather Than Tested

**The 1960s route to a heat shield thickness was arc-jet testing and margin.** [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998] write that PRIME's design procedures rested on a mathematical model and plasma arc testing and that its shield proved conservative. The modern route computes the material response, in [Arnold et al. 2013][research_arnold_2013], [Li et al. 2015e][research_li_2015_8], [Milos et al. 2015][research_milos_2015], [Chen 2016b][research_chen_2016], [Kumar and Mahulikar 2016b][research_kumar_mahulikar_2016_2], [Brune et al. 2017][research_brune_2017], [Harpale et al. 2018][research_harpale_2018], [Meurisse et al. 2018][research_meurisse_2018], [Cinquegrana et al. 2019][research_cinquegrana_2019], [Gulli and Maddalena 2019][research_gulli_maddalena_2019], [Rivier et al. 2019][research_rivier_2019], [Wang et al. 2019a][research_wang_2019_5], [Shilav and Khosid 2020][research_shilav_khosid_2020], [Raghunandan et al. 2021][research_pratibha_raghunandan_2021], [Hasan 2022][research_hasan_2022], [He et al. 2022b][research_he_2022], [Price et al. 2022][research_price_2022], [Chinnaraj et al. 2023b][research_chinnaraj_2023], [He et al. 2023][research_he_2023], [Lai and Leu 2023a][research_lai_leu_2023], [Lai and Leu 2023b][research_lai_leu_2023_2], [Scandelli et al. 2023][research_scandelli_2023], [Chen and Gökçen 2024][research_chen_gokcen_2024], [Yang et al. 2024][research_yang_2024_2], [Price et al. 2025][research_price_2025], [Wang et al. 2025a][research_wang_2025_3], [Cutrone et al. 2026][research_cutrone_2026], [Zibitsker and Martin 2026][research_zibitsker_martin_2026].

That is the largest single practical change in the subject. The cross-check performed earlier in this article, inverting a published thickness to recover an effective heat of ablation of 27.8 megajoules per kilogram, is the crude version of what a material response code now does properly, with pyrolysis chemistry, in-depth conduction and a quantified uncertainty on the answer. **Arc-jet testing did not go away. It became validation instead of design.**

### Lifting Bodies Came Back Mostly Uncrewed

The shape survived, and the clusters below on lifting bodies and the SV-5 family and on reusable launch vehicles, spaceplanes and booster return record that work.

**What is flying now is closer to PRIME than to the X-24A**, in the sense that it is mostly uncrewed and mostly automatic. Alongside them sits the deployable or inflatable aeroshell that packs small and opens to a large low-ballistic-coefficient decelerator. **That attacks the problem from the opposite end.** PRIME lowered its ballistic coefficient to 60 pounds per square foot by being light. A deployable aeroshell lowers it by growing.

### Catching Things in the Air Is Now Routine

**The part of PRIME that failed twice in three flights is the part that has been most thoroughly vindicated.** The cluster below on parachutes, decelerators and recovery documents that outcome.

Mid-air retrieval by helicopter has since been demonstrated on a returning orbital booster, in the [encyclopaedia entry on mid-air retrieval][ref_mid_air_retrieval], and the supersonic parachute work that Mars entry demanded has produced a decelerator literature far deeper than anything available in 1967. **The technique outlived the aerodynamics**, which is not the outcome anyone would have predicted from a programme that lost two vehicles to a main parachute that never left its container and to line cutters fitted without their charges, in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998].

### The Footprint Became a Safety Calculation

Here the inversion is at its sharpest, in [Falsone and Prandini 2017][research_falsone_prandini_2017], [Kim et al. 2018][research_kim_2018], [Lee et al. 2018][research_lee_2018_2], [Annaloro et al. 2020][research_annaloro_2020], [Braun et al. 2020][research_braun_2020_2], [Jorgensen and Sharf 2021][research_jorgensen_sharf_2021], [Santos and Sampaio 2021][research_santos_sampaio_2021], [Bohman et al. 2024][research_bohman_2024], [Chen et al. 2025e][research_chen_2025_6], [Chen et al. 2025g][research_chen_2025_7], [Jain and Hastings 2025][research_jain_hastings_2025], [Navaz and Ntantis 2026][research_navaz_ntantis_2026], [Park et al. 2026][research_park_2026], [Yuricich 2026][research_yuricich_2026].

**PRIME wanted a large footprint. Modern practice wants a small and precisely predicted one.** The reachable area treated above as a capability is, for a spent stage or a decaying satellite, a hazard to be bounded, and the same trajectory mathematics now serves debris casualty risk, controlled disposal and range safety. **A quantity computed to show what a vehicle could reach is now computed to prove what it cannot.**

### The Same Relations, on Other Planets

**Nor can the equation tell which planet it is being asked about**, and the cluster below on planetary and superorbital entry, descent and landing is the evidence.

The equilibrium glide with a different gravitational parameter and a different atmosphere is what every planetary entry and every aerocapture study solves. Mars is where the modern work concentrates, because it has enough atmosphere to matter and not enough to make entry easy, and because the crossrange question there is the same question PRIME asked, being whether a vehicle can reach a chosen site rather than wherever the ballistic track puts it.

### How It Flies, Computed to a Standard Nobody Had

Underneath all of it is the aerodynamic and aerothermodynamic prediction that the period could only estimate, surveyed below under hypersonic aerodynamics and under heating.

The decades between PRIME and the current revival were not empty, and 1,411 of the survey's research records were published between 1973 and 2009.

### What the Survey Shows

**The arithmetic has not moved at all.** Crossrange still goes as the square of the lift-to-drag ratio, the optimal bank angle is still 45 degrees, the footprint still goes as the cube, and the once-per-orbit requirement is still about a lift-to-drag ratio of one.

**What moved twice is the requirement.** It went from the Air Force wanting a spacecraft that could come home on the next pass, to nobody wanting that and crewed vehicles giving up ninety-one percent of the capability, to a different community wanting lateral range specifically because it defeats prediction.

**And the thing PRIME was worst at turned out to be the thing that lasted.** The programme lost two of three vehicles to the recovery system. Mid-air retrieval is now a demonstrated commercial technique, in the [encyclopaedia entry on mid-air retrieval][ref_mid_air_retrieval], and the aerodynamic configuration it was carrying is not flown by anyone.

### Parachutes, decelerators and recovery

**The recovery system and its descendants**, being parachutes and their deployment, inflation, reefing and fabrics, ballutes and inflatable or deployable decelerators, and the mid-air retrieval of a descending payload. It is the largest cluster, and it includes parachute engineering for aircraft, ordnance and personnel because they share the deployment and inflation problem. 135 of the 650 titles say supersonic and 161 name a ballute, an aeroshell or an inflatable or deployable decelerator.

### Hypersonic aerodynamics, flow fields and the boundary layer

**The flow the vehicle flies through**, being blunt-body and slender-body hypersonic aerodynamics, nonequilibrium and rarefied flow, the boundary layer and its transition, wakes, the plasma sheath and communications blackout, and the computational test cases of the double ellipse and the double ellipsoid.

### Entry guidance, trajectory optimisation and hypersonic flight control

**Steering an entry vehicle and computing the trajectory it should fly**, including predictor-corrector guidance, numerical trajectory optimisation and the attitude control of hypersonic vehicles. **277 of the 412 records date from 2010 or later.** 85 titles name a convex, pseudospectral, predictor-corrector, evolutionary, swarm, neural or learning method, which is what the free computation described above looks like in a title.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating PRIME through crossrange alone gets the programme wrong in at least three ways.**

**The vehicle was not only a manoeuvring experiment.** It carried a heat shield the programme wanted measured, and ASSET had already been devoted to structures and heating. The sources disagree on how far PRIME was a heating experiment. The official history lists the acquisition of heat shield and aerodynamic data first among the five flight objectives, in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998], while [Heppenheimer][ref_heppenheimer_1999] says that PRIME did not attempt to produce heating data because ASSET had covered it. Heating and manoeuvring were both objectives and the article's keystone selects one. The wider class of entry vehicles, most of which never manoeuvred at all, fills the survey's cluster on capsules and ballistic entry, and the field it sits inside is the survey as a whole.

**The equilibrium glide is not what it flew.** The model assumes a smooth glide that begins below circular speed. PRIME entered at 2.03 degrees from 400,000 feet, faster than the circular speed the model uses, and the programme's computed trajectory dips and oscillates rather than gliding in equilibrium, so it reached the crossrange it did under conditions the model describes only approximately, in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998]. That the numbers agree to one percent at the lower disputed lift-to-drag ratio is encouraging and is not proof.

**The reference area is derived, not published.** Everything in the thermal section inherits that. The crossrange result does not, and for that reason the crossrange is the keystone and the heating is not.

A fourth concerns the article's framing. **A vehicle whose recovery system failed twice in three flights is a programme about recovery at least as much as about entry**, and it gets one short section here.

## The Source Base

**The research survey holds 4,642 research records drawn from the Technical Reports Server of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA, from the Defense Technical Information Center and from the Crossref index**, of which 585 link to the NASA Technical Reports Server, 281 are Defense Technical Information Center reports by host or by that center's identifier prefix, and the remaining 3,776 are other records reached through Crossref. The report servers therefore hold 866 records, being 18.7 percent of the survey, and its median publication year is 2009.

**The subject has a deep period record.** Of the 4,554 research records that carry a year, 1,056, or 23.2 percent, predate 1976, which reflects that lifting entry was worked out in a concentrated burst between about 1958 and 1972 and then largely left alone until the current revival. **The period record names the subject in its own vocabulary.** Where the modern literature says crossrange, the period reports say lateral range, roll modulation and maneuvering range, and the period work is found under those words.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or on the Defense Technical Information Center's own host, or when it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The records this article's own argument rests on are report primaries under that rule**, among them the project's official history in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998], [Reed's history of the lifting bodies][research_r_dale_reed_1997], the X-24A data in [Cochrane and Graham][research_john_cochrane_kenneth_graham_1971] and [McTigue][research_john_g_mctigue_1970], and the planform figures in [Saltzman, Wang and Iliff][research_saltzman_2002]. **The rule does not reach the journal papers of the period**, such as the lateral range analyses published by the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, so 18.7 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Five subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the vehicle itself, by its own names | SV-5D, SV-5, X-23, X-23A, Project PRIME, PRIME vehicle, program, programme, reentry or re-entry | 3 |
| the bank angle that maximises crossrange | crossrange, cross range, lateral range together with bank, banking, roll, rolling | 2 |
| mid-air retrieval of a returning payload | mid air, midair, aerial recovery, aerial retrieval, in air capturing, in air capture, air snatch | 20 |
| the once-around recall requirement | once around, abort once, landing site access, recall, return to launch site, global landing | 2 |
| the effective heat of ablation | heat of ablation, heats of ablation, ablation heat | 0 |

**The vehicle itself is almost absent from the titles.** Three titles name it by SV-5, X-23 or PRIME. One is the project's official history in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998], one defines the entry environment of an assured crew return vehicle derived from the X-23 and X-24A in [Campbell et al. 1996a][research_campbell_caram_1996], and the third, of 2023, gives the designation X-23 to a hypersonic glide vehicle in its title, in [Butler et al. 2023][research_butler_benitez_2023]. The flight record this article reconstructs therefore rests on the official history and on Reed rather than on a technical literature of the vehicle.

**The bank angle that maximises crossrange has two titles, both of the period**, lateral range control by banking in [Baradell 1962][research_baradell_1962] and roll modulation for maximum lateral range in [Wagner 1965][research_wagner_1965]. The optimum of 45 degrees derived above is standard and is rarely the subject of a title.

**Mid-air retrieval has a small literature of its own.** Of the 20 titles, 5 concern returning boosters or reusable launch vehicles, and [Catch a Falling Star 1993][research_catch_a_1993] records the parachute lessons of the Air Force space capsule mid-air recovery programme from 1959 to 1985, the technique this article records as already in service for returning film capsules when PRIME flew.

**The recall requirement that motivated the vehicle has two titles**, abort-once-around dispersion in [Kyle 1975][research_kyle_1975] and global landing site access by skip trajectories in [Bryant 2002][research_bryant_2002]. The requirement's history is in [Heppenheimer][ref_heppenheimer_1999] rather than in a research literature.

**No title names the effective heat of ablation**, so the cross-check above that recovers 27.8 megajoules per kilogram from a published thickness stands on the relation shown rather than on a measured value in the survey.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** The programme acronyms do not identify its literature. PRIME collides with prime numbers and prime movers, and START with the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty and with the ordinary English verb, so neither word admits a record to the survey. Beyond the acronyms, footprint belongs to carbon, water and ecological accounting and to tyre contact, recovery to economics and to waste heat, ablation to medicine, to laser materials processing and to the ablators of inertial fusion targets, charring to fire science, and entry to almost everything. **Re-entry is also the return of prisoners to the community**, the subject of a large criminal justice literature, and a term of cardiac electrophysiology and of software, and parachute also names a golden parachute in finance, a heart valve malformation, a mine ventilation stopping and a game for schoolchildren.

**Several further families share this subject's words and nothing else.** Lateral motion of a vehicle is a term of art in railway dynamics and in road-vehicle lane keeping. Maneuvering range names an instrumented air combat facility off the East Coast, so the phrase also titles a construction quality assurance plan. Lateral range is also a term in search and detection theory. Glider, maneuvering and hovering all belong to underwater vehicles as well as to aircraft. **Guidance, landing and control are shared with tactical missiles, small unmanned aircraft, rotorcraft and spacecraft operating in orbit**, and a reading of this subject's titles removes records of all four. Impact-angle and homing guidance of tactical missiles, the landing and flight control of drones and multirotors, helicopter flight test, and rendezvous, formation flight and debris impact on orbit are excluded, because none of them concerns a vehicle returning through the atmosphere.

**Records that share a word with the subject and nothing else are excluded.** Beyond the families above, the excluded classes include road, rail and ground transport, clinical medicine and biology, ion, surface and plasma physics, robotics and manufacturing, building heating and energy systems, combustion, fire science, boiling, critical heat flux and industrial heat exchange, thermal analysis as a laboratory chemistry discipline, atmospheric remote sensing and radio propagation, boundary-layer meteorology, airline operations, generic fluid mechanics and numerical mathematics, satellite communications, and electronics and materials. Records that are not works are excluded as well, meaning figures, tables, supplementary files, peer-review reports, notices of erratum, correction, retraction or withdrawal, and journal front matter such as reviewer lists and indexes, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works. A review of a book, a reference or definition entry, a notice such as a news item, a press release or an editorial preface, and a second deposit of a document the survey already holds, such as a report server copy or a reprint of a journal article, are not admitted either, because none of them is a further research work.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept**, because they bear on entry, flight or the design of a vehicle like this one without being about it. They are spacecraft attitude control by reaction jets, wheels and gyroscopes, crew physiology during entry and landing, the entry heating of meteoroids and micrometeorites, lunar and planetary landing and the erosion a landing rocket causes, aircraft structural weight estimation, rocket engine components, the propulsive landing of returning boosters, and the air-breathing hypersonic vehicle control literature, whose vehicles fly the same speed range without returning from orbit. **Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, as reported by the accessible record.** The SV-5D PRIME was built by Martin Marietta for the United States Air Force under the START programme. Four were built, three were launched on SLV-3 Atlas boosters from Vandenberg on 21 December 1966, 5 March 1967 and 19 April 1967, and the fourth flight was cancelled on 12 May 1967. The first two were lost to recovery-system failures and the third was recovered in mid-air by a JC-130B at 12,000 feet. The crossranges flown were zero, 654 miles and more than 710 miles in the official history's narrative, taken here as 1,053 and 1,143 kilometres, while its summary table gives 499 and more than 710 nautical miles. The second flight held a constant bank of 46 degrees until terminal guidance. The third re-entered at 400,000 feet, 26,808 feet per second and 2.03 degrees, 1,360 nautical miles from launch. Martin's design figure for the hypersonic lift-to-drag ratio was 1.2 or better. All of this is in [Vitelli and Hallion][research_hallion_1998]. The vehicle was 6 feet 8 inches long, and its recorded weights run from about 800 to 895 pounds, with 894 used here. The surviving vehicle is at the National Museum of the United States Air Force.

**Historical fact, on the designation.** The nomenclature record shows a request for X-23A submitted on 16 November 1965 for the SV-5P, disapproved on 15 December 1965 on the stated ground that the aircraft was unmanned, and a late-1966 decision to seek X-23A for the SV-5D and X-24A for the SV-5P, of which only the second was ever submitted, in the [standard reference on designations][ref_designation_missing]. **This article reports that record and does not adjudicate between it and universal usage.**

**Engineering analysis, performed here and checkable.** The equilibrium-glide crossrange relation, its closed form, the optimal bank angle of 45 degrees, the required crossrange of half the ground-track spacing, and the resulting lift-to-drag requirement of 0.978 by the closed form and 1.018 by exact integration, are all derived in this article from stated assumptions. The simultaneous solution of downrange and crossrange for the bank angle and lift-to-drag ratio, and the inversion of crossrange alone at a documented bank angle, are likewise derived here. The heating figures follow from the Sutton and Graves correlation applied to the equilibrium-glide density.

**Inference, and flagged as such.** That the vehicle's effective lift-to-drag ratio through the manoeuvring phase was about 1.01 on the second flight and 1.05 on the third is an inference from the documented crossranges at the documented bank angles under the equilibrium-glide model. It rises to about 1.14 if the summary table's nautical miles are right, and it lies between the programme's trim curve at the flown angle of attack and that curve's maximum, below Martin's design figure of 1.2. The simultaneous solution of downrange and crossrange is not used as a measurement, because at the documented boost range it demands a bank angle the record contradicts. That nobody submitted the X-23A request because the 1965 refusal had said unmanned vehicles need none is a reading offered by the designation reference and is not documented.

**Assumptions that everything downstream inherits.** The reference area of 1.386 square metres is scaled from the X-24A and is not published for this vehicle. The entry speed of 25,200 feet per second, the nose radius of 0.1 metres, the hypersonic drag coefficient of unity, the ablator density of 550 kilograms per cubic metre, the parachute drag coefficient of 0.75, and the nominal lift-to-drag ratios of the capsules and the Space Shuttle orbiter in the comparison table are all assumed. The record's own speeds run from 21,853 to 26,808 feet per second.

**What the record does not settle.** The vehicle's lift-to-drag ratio in flight, beyond what the programme's trim curve shows. Its actual reference area. Whether the crossranges are statute or nautical miles. The bank angle flown on the third flight. The stagnation heat load, which the programme's stated figure and its computed heating curve give very differently. The peak deceleration and heating as measured, which were certainly telemetered and are not in the accessible literature. And the reason the X-23A request was never sent.

## Out of Scope

The ASSET phase of the START programme, which deserves its own treatment. The Atlas SLV-3 as a launch vehicle. The X-24A and X-24B, which follow in this series. The mid-air retrieval technique and its origins in satellite film return. The detailed chemistry of charring ablators. The Space Shuttle crossrange requirement's full political history, of which only the arithmetic is treated here.

## Conclusion

**PRIME asked whether a spacecraft could steer on the way home, and the answer was yes, by about a thousand kilometres.**

The number matters more than it looks. A returning vehicle needs roughly half a ground-track spacing of crossrange to reach a chosen site without waiting, and at the equator that requires a lift-to-drag ratio of 0.978 by the relation the period used and 1.018 when the approximation in that relation is removed. **A lifting body near unity is therefore not a modest capability but the threshold one**, and the difference between it and a ballistic capsule is not a matter of degree. One can come home when it chooses and the other cannot.

One more measure shows how steeply that capability is bought. The reachable ground area scales as the crossrange half-width times the downrange depth, and those go as the square and the first power of the lift-to-drag ratio respectively, so

$$
A_\text{footprint} \propto \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)^3
\tag{87}
$$

**The footprint goes as the cube.** Raising the ratio from 1.0 to 1.2 enlarges the region a vehicle can reach by a factor of 1.73. Twenty percent of lift-to-drag ratio was therefore worth arguing about, and the disagreement in the sources matters.

The vehicle that demonstrated this weighed 894 pounds, flew three times, was lost twice on the way back, and carries a designation that was never requested for it. **All four of those facts deserve to be kept.**

This section collects the 87 display equations of the article in the order they appear,
each under its number and reproduced exactly as it stands in the text.
A title in bold names an established result,
and a title in italics beginning with the word Bespoke names a construction made for this analysis.
Of the 87, 55 are established and 32 are bespoke.
Mechanics are in International System units, with distances in metres or kilometres and speeds in metres per second, while the record quotes feet, statute miles, nautical miles and British thermal units, so each conversion is stated where it is made, and the entry speed of 25,200 feet per second, the working weight of 894 pounds and the derived reference area of 1.386 square metres are values the article assumes.

**Equation 1, Lift-to-Drag Ratio.**
The lift-to-drag ratio is the ratio of lift to drag, equal to the ratio of the lift and drag coefficients.
[encyclopaedia entry on the lift-to-drag ratio][ref_lift_to_drag]

$$
\frac{L}{D} = \frac{C_L}{C_D}
\tag{1}
$$

**Equation 2, Cost of PRIME Relative to the X-20.**
The documented 70 million dollars of the Precision Recovery Including Maneuvering Entry programme against the 458 million dollars of the cancelled X-20 is a ratio of about one seventh.
[Reed][research_r_dale_reed_1997]
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
\frac{70}{458} = 0.153
\tag{2}
$$

*Equation 3, Bespoke Departure of the Working Weight from the Lift-Off Weight.*
The working weight of 894 pounds that the article chooses among conflicting figures differs from the first vehicle's documented lift-off weight of 895 pounds by about one tenth of a percent.

$$
\frac{895}{894} - 1 = 0.11\%
\tag{3}
$$

*Equation 4, Bespoke Planform Fill Ratio of the X-24A.*
The article defines the ratio of planform area to the product of length and span and evaluates it on the X-24A at about 0.58.
[Saltzman, Wang and Iliff][research_saltzman_2002]

$$
k_S = \frac{S_\text{X-24A}}{l\,b} = \frac{195.0}{24.50 \times 13.63} = 0.5839
\tag{4}
$$

*Equation 5, Bespoke Reference Area of the SV-5D.*
Applying the X-24A planform fill ratio to the length and span of the SV-5D assumes that the two shapes fill their bounding boxes alike and gives about 1.39 square metres.

$$
S = k_S\, l\, b = 0.5839 \times 2.032 \times 1.168 = 1.386\ \text{m}^2
\tag{5}
$$

*Equation 6, Bespoke Planform Fill Ratio from an Alternative Source.*
The same fill ratio evaluated on the alternative X-24A dimensions is about 0.58, which makes the derived area 1.1 percent smaller.
[McTigue][research_john_g_mctigue_1970]

$$
\frac{191}{24.5 \times 13.5} = 0.5775
\tag{6}
$$

**Equation 7, Linear Scale Ratio of the SV-5D to the X-24A.**
The ratio of the documented lengths of the two vehicles is about 0.27.

$$
\frac{l_\text{SV-5D}}{l_\text{X-24A}} = \frac{2.032}{7.47} = 0.272
\tag{7}
$$

**Equation 8, Weight Ratios of the SV-5D to the X-24A.**
The documented SV-5D weight is 7.5 percent of the X-24A launch weight and 16 percent of its empty weight.
[Reed][research_r_dale_reed_1997]
[Cochrane and Graham][research_john_cochrane_kenneth_graham_1971]

$$
\frac{894}{12{,}000} = 0.075, \qquad \frac{894}{5{,}500} = 0.163
\tag{8}
$$

**Equation 9, Radial Force Balance in a Gliding Entry.**
In the radial direction the vertical component of the rolled lift and the centrifugal force of the curved path together support the weight.

$$
L\cos\phi + \frac{m V^2}{R} = W
\tag{9}
$$

**Equation 10, Equilibrium Glide Lift Requirement.**
With the centrifugal term written through the speed as a fraction of circular speed, the lift a gliding vehicle needs is its weight less the part its speed already carries.

$$
L\cos\phi = W\left(1 - \bar V^2\right)
\tag{10}
$$

**Equation 11, Lift Required at Three Quarters of Circular Speed.**
At three quarters of circular speed the equilibrium glide needs a vertical lift of 0.44 of the weight.

$$
1 - 0.75^2 = 0.4375
\tag{11}
$$

**Equation 12, Circular Satellite Speed at the Surface.**
Equating gravitational and centripetal acceleration at the mean Earth radius with standard gravity gives a circular speed of about 7,900 metres per second.

$$
V_c = \sqrt{g R} = \sqrt{9.80665 \times 6.371\times 10^6} = 7{,}904\ \text{m/s}
\tag{12}
$$

**Equation 13, Equations of Motion Along and Across the Path.**
Drag decelerates the vehicle along its path and the sideways component of the rolled lift turns its heading.

$$
m\frac{dV}{dt} = -D, \qquad m V \frac{d\psi}{dt} = L\sin\phi
\tag{13}
$$

**Equation 14, Heading Change per Unit Speed.**
Dividing the turning equation by the deceleration and substituting the force balance leaves a heading rate per unit speed that depends on the vehicle only through its lift-to-drag ratio.
[Vinh's treatment of atmospheric flight trajectories][book_vinh_1981]
[Regan and Anandakrishnan on re-entry dynamics][book_regan_anandakrishnan_1993]

$$
\frac{d\psi}{dV} = -\frac{L}{D}\,\frac{\sin\phi}{V}
\tag{14}
$$

**Equation 15, Heading Change in an Equilibrium Glide.**
Integrating from the entry speed gives a heading change proportional to the logarithm of the speed ratio at constant bank and lift-to-drag ratio.
[Vinh's treatment of atmospheric flight trajectories][book_vinh_1981]
[Regan and Anandakrishnan on re-entry dynamics][book_regan_anandakrishnan_1993]

$$
\psi(V) = \frac{L}{D}\sin\phi \, \ln\frac{V_e}{V}
\tag{15}
$$

**Equation 16, Heading Change from Circular to Quarter Circular Speed.**
At Martin's design lift-to-drag ratio of 1.2 and a bank of 45 degrees, slowing to a quarter of circular speed turns the vehicle through about 67 degrees.

$$
\psi = 1.2 \times \sin 45^\circ \times \ln 4 = 1.176\ \text{rad} = 67.4^\circ
\tag{16}
$$

**Equation 17, Crossrange Rate per Unit Speed in the Small-Angle Form.**
Dividing the lateral rate by the deceleration with the heading taken as small, the step the period literature took, gives the crossrange accumulated per unit speed.

$$
\frac{dy}{dV} = -\,\frac{V\psi\,(L/D)\cos\phi}{g\left(1-\bar V^2\right)}
\tag{17}
$$

**Equation 18, Substitution in the Squared Speed Fraction.**
Writing the speed through the squared speed fraction $u$ and gravity through the circular speed prepares every factor of circular speed to cancel.

$$
V = V_c\sqrt{u}, \qquad dV = \frac{V_c}{2\sqrt{u}}\,du, \qquad g = \frac{V_c^2}{R}
\tag{18}
$$

**Equation 19, Crossrange Increment in the Squared Speed Fraction.**
After the substitution the crossrange increment depends on the Earth radius, the lift-to-drag ratio, the bank and the heading alone.

$$
dy = -\frac{R}{2}\,\frac{L}{D}\cos\phi\,\frac{\psi\,du}{1-u}
\tag{19}
$$

**Equation 20, Closed Crossrange Integral.**
Substituting the logarithmic heading solution turns the accumulated crossrange into the Earth radius times the squared lift-to-drag ratio, a bank factor and a single integral in the entry speed fraction.

$$
y = \frac{R}{4}\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)^2 \sin\phi\cos\phi \; I(u_e), \qquad I(u_e) = \int_0^{u_e} \frac{\ln(u_e/u)}{1-u}\,du
\tag{20}
$$

**Equation 21, Geometric Series Expansion.**
The reciprocal of one minus $u$ expands as a geometric series that converges for $u$ below one.

$$
\frac{1}{1-u} = \sum_{n\ge 0} u^n \qquad \text{for} \quad 0 \le u < 1
\tag{21}
$$

**Equation 22, Logarithmic Moment Integral.**
Each term of the expanded integrand integrates to the reciprocal square of one more than its power.

$$
\int_0^1 (-\ln u)\,u^n\,du = \frac{1}{(n+1)^2}
\tag{22}
$$

**Equation 23, Crossrange Integral at Circular Entry as the Basel Sum.**
For entry at circular speed the integral is the sum of reciprocal squares, which equals $\pi^2/6$.

$$
I(1) = \int_0^1 \frac{-\ln u}{1-u}\,du = \sum_{k\ge 1} \frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6} = 1.6449
\tag{23}
$$

**Equation 24, Double-Angle Identity for the Bank Factor.**
The product of the sine and cosine of the bank angle is half the sine of twice the angle.

$$
\sin\phi\cos\phi = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\phi
\tag{24}
$$

**Equation 25, Stationarity Condition of the Bank Factor.**
The first derivative of the bank factor vanishes where the cosine of twice the bank is zero and the second derivative there is negative, so the point is a maximum.

$$
\frac{d}{d\phi}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2\phi\right) = \cos 2\phi = 0, \qquad \frac{d^2}{d\phi^2} = -2\sin 2\phi = -2 < 0
\tag{25}
$$

**Equation 26, Optimum Bank Angle for Crossrange.**
Crossrange is maximised at a bank of 45 degrees, where the bank factor is one half, independent of the vehicle.

$$
\phi_\text{opt} = 45^\circ, \qquad \sin\phi\cos\phi = \tfrac{1}{2}
\tag{26}
$$

**Equation 27, Maximum Crossrange of an Equilibrium Glide.**
Combining the optimum bank with the circular-entry integral gives a maximum crossrange equal to $\pi^2/48$ of the Earth radius times the square of the lift-to-drag ratio.

$$
\frac{y_\text{max}}{R} = \frac{\pi^2}{48}\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)^2 = 0.2056\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)^2
\tag{27}
$$

**Equation 28, Maximum Crossrange at a Lift-to-Drag Ratio of 1.2.**
At Martin's design ratio of 1.2 the closed form gives about 1,890 kilometres of crossrange from circular entry.

$$
y_\text{max} = 0.2056 \times 1.2^2 \times 6.371\times 10^6 = 1.886\times 10^6\ \text{m} = 1{,}019\ \text{nmi}
\tag{28}
$$

*Equation 29, Bespoke Final Heading at the End of the Glide.*
Evaluating the heading solution at a glide end taken by the article as one percent of circular speed shows the heading passing half a turn for ratios near one.

$$
\psi_\text{end} = \frac{L}{D}\sin 45^\circ \ln\frac{V_e}{0.01\,V_c}
\tag{29}
$$

**Equation 30, Speed at Which the Heading Reaches Half a Turn.**
Lateral displacement stops accumulating where the sine of the heading returns to zero, which the logarithmic heading solution places at a speed exponentially small in the reciprocal of the ratio times the bank sine.

$$
\sin\psi = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \psi = 180^\circ, \qquad V_{180} = V_e\exp\left(-\frac{\pi}{(L/D)\sin\phi}\right)
\tag{30}
$$

**Equation 31, Sidereal Rotation Rate of the Earth.**
The rotation rate relative to the fixed stars is two pi radians per sidereal day of 86,164 seconds.

$$
\omega_E = \frac{2\pi}{86{,}164\ \text{s}} = 7.292\times 10^{-5}\ \text{rad/s}
\tag{31}
$$

*Equation 32, Bespoke Ground Track Spacing in Longitude.*
The Earth turns through about 22.6 degrees in one orbit for a period the article takes as a nominal 90 minutes.

$$
\Delta\lambda = \omega_E T = 7.292\times 10^{-5} \times 5400 = 0.3937\ \text{rad} = 22.56^\circ
\tag{32}
$$

*Equation 33, Bespoke Ground Track Spacing at the Equator.*
The longitude spacing of the nominal 90 minute orbit becomes about 2,510 kilometres of ground distance at the equator.

$$
d = R\,\Delta\lambda = 6.371\times 10^6 \times 0.3937 = 2{,}509\ \text{km}
\tag{33}
$$

*Equation 34, Bespoke Once-per-Orbit Crossrange Requirement.*
The article requires that any site be reached on one pass or the next, which sets the crossrange at half the equatorial track spacing of the nominal 90 minute orbit.

$$
y_\text{req} = \tfrac{1}{2} R\,\Delta\lambda = 1{,}254\ \text{km}
\tag{34}
$$

*Equation 35, Bespoke Required Lift-to-Drag Ratio in Closed Form.*
Inverting the maximum crossrange relation on the once-per-orbit requirement gives a required lift-to-drag ratio of about 0.98.

$$
\frac{L}{D} = \sqrt{\frac{y_\text{req}/R}{\pi^2/48}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.1968}{0.2056}} = 0.978
\tag{35}
$$

*Equation 36, Bespoke Required Lift-to-Drag Ratio by Exact Integration.*
Bisecting the exact integration against the same requirement, rather than using the small-angle closed form, gives a required ratio of about 1.02.

$$
\left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{exact} = 1.018
\tag{36}
$$

*Equation 37, Bespoke Latitude Dependence of the Requirement.*
Because the track spacing carries the cosine of latitude, the once-per-orbit requirement falls with latitude and the required ratio falls with its square root.

$$
y_\text{req}(\varphi) = \tfrac{1}{2} R\,\Delta\lambda\cos\varphi, \qquad \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{req}(\varphi) = \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)_\text{req}(0)\sqrt{\cos\varphi}
\tag{37}
$$

**Equation 38, Crossrange Ratio between the Disputed Lift-to-Drag Ratios.**
Because crossrange goes as the square of the ratio, the twenty percent difference between 1.2 and 1.0 becomes a forty-four percent difference in crossrange.

$$
\frac{y(1.2)}{y(1.0)} = \left(\frac{1.2}{1.0}\right)^2 = 1.44
\tag{38}
$$

**Equation 39, Haversine Great-Circle Distance.**
The haversine formula gives the great-circle distance between Vandenberg Air Force Base and the recovery area near Kwajalein as about 7,790 kilometres.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
d = 2R\arcsin\sqrt{\sin^2\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2} + \cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\sin^2\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}} = 7{,}787\ \text{km}
\tag{39}
$$

**Equation 40, Downrange Rate per Unit Speed.**
Dividing the along-path rate by the deceleration gives the downrange accumulated per unit speed in the equilibrium glide.

$$
\frac{dx}{dV} = -\frac{V\,(L/D)\cos\phi}{g\left(1-u\right)}
\tag{40}
$$

**Equation 41, Downrange Increment in the Squared Speed Fraction.**
The same substitution cancels every factor of circular speed and leaves an elementary integrand.

$$
dx = -\frac{R}{2}\,\frac{L}{D}\cos\phi\,\frac{du}{1-u}
\tag{41}
$$

**Equation 42, Downrange of an Equilibrium Glide.**
Integrating gives a downrange linear in the lift-to-drag ratio and logarithmic in one over one minus the entry speed fraction.

$$
x = \frac{L}{D}\cos\phi \;\frac{R}{2}\ln\frac{1}{1-u_e}
\tag{42}
$$

**Equation 43, Downrange Lost at the Optimum Bank.**
Banking at 45 degrees costs the fraction one minus the cosine of the bank, about twenty-nine percent, of the downrange flown wings level.

$$
1 - \cos 45^\circ = 0.293
\tag{43}
$$

*Equation 44, Bespoke Pair Solve for Bank and Lift-to-Drag Ratio.*
The article treats the documented crossrange and downrange as two equations and divides one by the square of the other to recover the bank angle and then the ratio, an inversion that rests on the entry speed and boost range it assumes.

$$
\tan\phi = \frac{y/B}{(x/A)^2}, \qquad \frac{L}{D} = \frac{x/A}{\cos\phi}
\tag{44}
$$

*Equation 45, Bespoke Exact Model Errors at the Disputed Ratios.*
The exact model, flown from the assumed entry speed, under-predicts the demonstrated 1,143 kilometres by 8.8 percent at a ratio of 1.0 and over-predicts it by 27 percent at 1.2.

$$
\frac{1{,}042.7}{1{,}143} - 1 = -8.8\%, \qquad \frac{1{,}452.9}{1{,}143} - 1 = +27\%
\tag{45}
$$

*Equation 46, Bespoke Exact Crossrange at Martin's Design Ratio.*
The exact integration from circular speed at a ratio of 1.2 gives 1,696 kilometres, which converts to about 1,054 statute miles, close to Martin's claim of 1,000 miles.

$$
\frac{1{,}696}{1.609} = 1{,}054\ \text{statute miles}
\tag{46}
$$

**Equation 47, Documented Boost Range in Kilometres.**
The 1,360 nautical miles from launch to entry interface on the ground-track chart is about 2,519 kilometres.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
1{,}360 \times 1.852 = 2{,}518.7\ \text{km}
\tag{47}
$$

**Equation 48, Documented Entry Speed Fraction Above Unity.**
The documented entry speed of 26,808 feet per second exceeds circular speed, so the squared speed fraction is above one, where the downrange relation has no finite value.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
u_e = \left(\frac{26{,}808}{25{,}933}\right)^2 = 1.069 > 1
\tag{48}
$$

*Equation 49, Bespoke Exact Crossrange Inversions at a Documented Bank.*
At the second flight's documented bank of 46 degrees the exact integration from the assumed entry speed needs ratios of 1.007 and 1.053 to reach the second and third flight crossranges.

$$
y_\text{exact}\left(1.007,\ 46^\circ\right) = 1{,}052.5\ \text{km}, \qquad y_\text{exact}\left(1.053,\ 46^\circ\right) = 1{,}142.6\ \text{km}
\tag{49}
$$

**Equation 50, Third Flight Crossrange Read as Nautical Miles.**
Read as nautical miles, the 710 miles of the third flight is about 1,315 kilometres.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
710 \times 1.852 = 1{,}314.9\ \text{km}
\tag{50}
$$

**Equation 51, Equilibrium Glide Density and Lift Parameter.**
The equilibrium glide force balance fixes the density at each speed in terms of the lift parameter, the weight per unit lifting area.

$$
\rho = \frac{2\beta_L(1-u)}{V^2\cos\phi}, \qquad \beta_L = \frac{W}{S\,C_L}
\tag{51}
$$

**Equation 52, Ballistic Coefficient.**
The ballistic coefficient is the weight divided by the product of reference area and drag coefficient.

$$
\beta = \frac{W}{S\,C_D}
\tag{52}
$$

**Equation 53, Ratio of Ballistic Coefficient to Lift Parameter.**
The ballistic coefficient and the lift parameter stand in the ratio of the lift to the drag coefficient, which is the lift-to-drag ratio.

$$
\frac{\beta}{\beta_L} = \frac{C_L}{C_D} = \frac{L}{D}
\tag{53}
$$

*Equation 54, Bespoke Ballistic Coefficient of the SV-5D.*
The working weight on the derived reference area at an assumed hypersonic drag coefficient of one gives a ballistic coefficient of about 2,870 newtons per square metre.

$$
\beta = \frac{3{,}977}{1.386 \times 1.0} = 2{,}869\ \text{N/m}^2 = 60\ \text{lb/ft}^2
\tag{54}
$$

**Equation 55, Sutton and Graves Stagnation Heating.**
The Sutton and Graves relation gives the stagnation-point convective heat flux as a constant times the square root of density over nose radius times the cube of speed, in metric units for air.

$$
\dot q_s = k\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{R_n}}\,V^3, \qquad k = 1.7415\times 10^{-4}
\tag{55}
$$

**Equation 56, Stagnation Heating Along the Equilibrium Glide.**
Substituting the glide density makes the stagnation heat flux proportional to $u\sqrt{1-u}$.

$$
\dot q_s \propto \sqrt{\frac{1-u}{u}}\;u^{3/2} = u\sqrt{1-u}
\tag{56}
$$

**Equation 57, Condition for Peak Stagnation Heating.**
Setting the derivative of the squared heating function to zero places its maximum at a squared speed fraction of two thirds.

$$
\frac{d}{du}\left[u^2(1-u)\right] = 2u - 3u^2 = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad u = \tfrac{2}{3}
\tag{57}
$$

**Equation 58, Speed of Peak Stagnation Heating.**
Peak heating in an equilibrium glide falls at about 82 percent of circular speed, about 6,450 metres per second, for any vehicle.

$$
u = \tfrac{2}{3}, \qquad V = 0.8165\,V_c = 6{,}454\ \text{m/s}
\tag{58}
$$

*Equation 59, Bespoke Density at Peak Heating.*
The glide balance at the derived lift parameter of 2,391 newtons per square metre and a bank of 45 degrees gives the density at the peak heating speed.

$$
\rho = \frac{2 \times 2{,}391 \times \tfrac{1}{3}}{6{,}454^2 \times \cos 45^\circ} = 5.41\times 10^{-5}\ \text{kg/m}^3
\tag{59}
$$

*Equation 60, Bespoke Peak Stagnation Heat Flux.*
The Sutton and Graves relation at the peak heating speed and density with a nose radius the article assumes as 0.1 metres gives about 109 watts per square centimetre.

$$
\dot q_{s,\text{max}} = 1.7415\times 10^{-4}\sqrt{\frac{5.41\times 10^{-5}}{0.1}}\,\left(6{,}454\right)^3 = 109\ \text{W/cm}^2
\tag{60}
$$

**Equation 61, Flight Heating Rate in Watts per Square Centimetre.**
The heating rate of 480 British thermal units per square foot per second read from the programme's figure is about 545 watts per square centimetre.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
480 \times 1.1357 = 545\ \text{W/cm}^2
\tag{61}
$$

*Equation 62, Bespoke Altitude of Peak Heating.*
Inverting an exponential atmosphere of an assumed scale height of 7,160 metres at the inferred peak heating density places the peak near 72 kilometres.

$$
h = -H\ln\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = -7{,}160\ln\left(4.42\times 10^{-5}\right) = 71.8\ \text{km}
\tag{62}
$$

**Equation 63, Stagnation Heat Load of an Equilibrium Glide.**
Integrating the Sutton and Graves flux over the glide in closed form gives the stagnation heat load in terms of the lift-to-drag ratio, the bank, the lift parameter, the nose radius and the entry speed fraction.

$$
Q = k\,\frac{L}{D}\sqrt{\cos\phi}\sqrt{\frac{2\beta_L}{R_n}}\frac{V_c^3}{g}\cdot\frac{\arcsin a - a\sqrt{1-a^2}}{2}
\tag{63}
$$

*Equation 64, Bespoke Duration of the Equilibrium Glide.*
Integrating the time over the glide from the assumed entry speed of 25,200 feet per second at a ratio of 1.2 and a bank of 45 degrees gives about 24 minutes.

$$
t = \frac{L}{D}\cos\phi\,\frac{V_c}{g}\,\text{artanh}\,\sqrt{u_e} = 1{,}452\ \text{s}
\tag{64}
$$

**Equation 65, Effective Heat of Ablation.**
The effective heat of ablation is the heat load divided by the areal mass of the heat shield.

$$
H_\text{eff} = \frac{Q}{\rho_\text{abl}\,t_\text{abl}}
\tag{65}
$$

*Equation 66, Bespoke Heat of Ablation at the Thick Shield.*
The model heat load over a shield of 2.75 inches at an assumed charring-ablator density of 550 kilograms per cubic metre implies about 28 megajoules per kilogram.

$$
\rho_\text{abl}t_\text{abl} = 550 \times 0.0699 = 38.4\ \text{kg/m}^2, \qquad H_\text{eff} = \frac{1.067\times 10^9}{38.4} = 27.8\ \text{MJ/kg}
\tag{66}
$$

**Equation 67, Documented Stagnation Heat Load in Metric Units.**
The documented 7,000 British thermal units per square foot is about 7.95 kilojoules per square centimetre.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
7{,}000 \times 11{,}357 = 7.95\times 10^7\ \text{J/m}^2 = 7.95\ \text{kJ/cm}^2
\tag{67}
$$

**Equation 68, Floor on the Heat Load from the Flight Heating Curve.**
A heating rate above 160 British thermal units per square foot per second for more than 300 seconds, read from the programme's figure, implies a heat load of at least 48,000 British thermal units per square foot.

$$
160 \times 300 = 48{,}000\ \text{BTU/ft}^2
\tag{68}
$$

**Equation 69, Deceleration in an Equilibrium Glide.**
The glide balance gives a deceleration in units of gravity of one minus the squared speed fraction over the lift-to-drag ratio times the cosine of bank.

$$
\frac{a}{g} = \frac{1-u}{(L/D)\cos\phi}
\tag{69}
$$

*Equation 70, Bespoke Deceleration at Entry.*
At the squared speed fraction of 0.944 that the assumed entry speed of 25,200 feet per second implies, the deceleration is about 0.07 of gravity.

$$
\frac{a}{g} = \frac{1 - 0.944}{1.2\cos 45^\circ} = 0.066
\tag{70}
$$

**Equation 71, Deceleration at the End of the Glide.**
As the speed fraction falls to zero the deceleration at a ratio of 1.2 and a bank of 45 degrees rises to about 1.18 of gravity.

$$
\frac{a}{g} = \frac{1}{1.2\cos 45^\circ} = 1.18
\tag{71}
$$

*Equation 72, Bespoke Allen and Eggers Peak Ballistic Deceleration.*
The Allen and Eggers peak deceleration of a ballistic entry from the documented entry state, with the scale height the article assumes as 7,160 metres, is about 6.2 of gravity.
[official history of the project][research_hallion_1998]

$$
a_\text{max} = \frac{V_e^2\sin\gamma_e}{2eH} = \frac{\left(8{,}171\right)^2\sin 2.03^\circ}{2e \times 7{,}160} = 60.8\ \text{m/s}^2 = 6.20\ g
\tag{72}
$$

*Equation 73, Bespoke Ratio of Ballistic to Lifting Peak Deceleration.*
The ballistic peak deceleration is about five times the lifting one, a ratio that inherits the assumed scale height.

$$
\frac{6.20}{1.18} = 5.25
\tag{73}
$$

**Equation 74, Speed of Sound at Ballute Deployment.**
At the standard atmosphere temperature of 226.5 kelvin at 30.4 kilometres the speed of sound is about 302 metres per second.

$$
a = \sqrt{\gamma R_\text{air} T} = \sqrt{1.4 \times 287 \times 226.5} = 302\ \text{m/s}
\tag{74}
$$

**Equation 75, Dynamic Pressure at Ballute Deployment.**
At Mach 2 and the standard atmosphere density at deployment altitude the dynamic pressure is about 3,350 pascals.

$$
q = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.0184 \times 603^2 = 3{,}350\ \text{Pa} = 70\ \text{lb/ft}^2
\tag{75}
$$

**Equation 76, Area of the Recovery Parachute.**
The documented 47 foot canopy diameter gives a nominal area of about 161 square metres.

$$
S_p = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi \times 14.33^2}{4} = 161\ \text{m}^2
\tag{76}
$$

*Equation 77, Bespoke Descent Rate under the Recovery Parachute.*
The terminal descent rate of the working weight under the canopy at sea level with an assumed drag coefficient of 0.75 is about 7.3 metres per second.

$$
V_d = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{\rho\,C_D S_p}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 3{,}977}{1.225 \times 0.75 \times 161}} = 7.33\ \text{m/s}
\tag{77}
$$

*Equation 78, Bespoke Descent Rate at 10,000 Feet.*
Scaling the descent rate by the square root of the standard atmosphere density ratio to 10,000 feet gives 28 feet per second at the assumed drag coefficient.

$$
V_d = 7.33\sqrt{\frac{1.225}{0.9046}} = 8.53\ \text{m/s} = 28.0\ \text{ft/s}
\tag{78}
$$

*Equation 79, Bespoke Drag Coefficient for the Specified Descent Rate.*
The documented 25 feet per second at 10,000 feet requires a drag coefficient of about 0.94 for the working weight on the nominal canopy area.

$$
C_D = 0.75\left(\frac{28.0}{25}\right)^2 = 0.94
\tag{79}
$$

**Equation 80, Unit Conversions of the Quoted Entry Speeds.**
The quoted entry speeds of 14,900 miles an hour and 26,808 feet per second convert to 21,853 feet per second and 18,278 miles an hour.

$$
14{,}900\ \text{mph} = 21{,}853\ \text{ft/s}, \qquad 26{,}808\ \text{ft/s} = 18{,}278\ \text{mph}
\tag{80}
$$

*Equation 81, Bespoke Launch Site Displacement in One Orbit.*
Vandenberg moves through the full track spacing of the nominal 90 minute orbit at its own latitude, about 2,060 kilometres.

$$
d_\text{VAFB} = R\,\Delta\lambda\cos\varphi = 6.371\times 10^6 \times 0.3937 \times \cos 34.74^\circ = 2{,}061\ \text{km}
\tag{81}
$$

*Equation 82, Bespoke Agreement with the Shuttle Crossrange Requirement.*
The displacement from the nominal 90 minute orbit agrees with the stated 1,100 nautical mile requirement to 1.2 percent.

$$
\frac{2{,}061 - 2{,}037}{2{,}037} = 1.2\ \text{percent}
\tag{82}
$$

**Equation 83, Lift-to-Drag Ratio for the Shuttle Crossrange Requirement.**
Putting the stated 1,100 nautical mile requirement through the closed-form maximum crossrange relation gives a required ratio of about 1.25.
[Heppenheimer's history of the Space Shuttle decision][ref_heppenheimer_1999]

$$
\frac{L}{D} = \sqrt{\frac{2{,}037/6{,}371}{0.2056}} = 1.25
\tag{83}
$$

**Equation 84, Demonstrated Fraction of the Shuttle Requirement.**
The demonstrated 1,143 kilometres is 56 percent of the 2,037 kilometre Shuttle requirement.

$$
\frac{1{,}143}{2{,}037} = 0.56
\tag{84}
$$

*Equation 85, Bespoke Crossrange of a Blunt Capsule.*
The closed form at a capsule lift-to-drag ratio the article assumes as a nominal 0.3 gives about 118 kilometres of crossrange.

$$
y = \pi^2/48 \times 0.3^2 \times 6.371\times 10^6 = 118\ \text{km}
\tag{85}
$$

*Equation 86, Bespoke Capsule Fraction of the Once-per-Orbit Requirement.*
The capsule's crossrange by exact integration is about nine percent of the once-per-orbit requirement of the nominal 90 minute orbit.

$$
\frac{117}{1{,}254} = 0.09
\tag{86}
$$

*Equation 87, Bespoke Footprint Scaling with Lift-to-Drag Ratio.*
Taking the reachable area as the crossrange half-width times the downrange depth, the article finds it grows as the cube of the lift-to-drag ratio.

$$
A_\text{footprint} \propto \left(\frac{L}{D}\right)^3
\tag{87}
$$

### Notation

- $L$, the lift
- $D$, the drag, and in Equation 76 the parachute diameter
- $C_L$, the lift coefficient
- $C_D$, the drag coefficient
- $k_S$, the ratio of planform area to the product of length and span
- $\phi$, the bank angle, the angle through which the lift vector is rolled from vertical
- $\bar V$, the speed as a fraction of circular satellite speed
- $V_c$, the circular satellite speed at the surface
- $V_e$, the entry speed
- $R$, the mean radius of the Earth
- $\psi$, the heading angle
- $u$, the square of the speed as a fraction of circular speed, with $u_e$ its value at entry
- $y$, the crossrange, with $y_\text{max}$ its maximum and $y_\text{req}$ the requirement
- $x$, the downrange
- $\omega_E$, the sidereal rotation rate of the Earth
- $\Delta\lambda$, the spacing in longitude of successive ground tracks
- $\varphi$, the latitude
- $\beta_L$, the lift parameter, the weight per unit area per unit lift coefficient
- $\beta$, the ballistic coefficient
- $\dot q_s$, the stagnation-point heat flux
- $R_n$, the nose radius
- $H$, the atmospheric scale height
- $Q$, the stagnation heat load
- $H_\text{eff}$, the effective heat of ablation
- $\rho$, the air density
- $\gamma_e$, the flight path angle at entry
- $S_p$, the nominal area of the recovery parachute
- $V_d$, the descent rate under the parachute
